passage: Rehana, sit. You're nervous about Monday's viva, I can see it. Let me tell you about mine. I was twenty, in Aligarh, in a room with three professors and one creaking ceiling fan. The first question was easy, about soil. And my mind went white, like a slate wiped clean. My hands were stuck to my knees and my throat was dry. The longest silence of my life. Then I remembered my father saying, when you are frightened, breathe out longer than you breathe in. So I did, twice. And I said it aloud: "Forgive me, my mind has gone blank. May I start again?" The oldest professor nodded. "Take your time, Miss Parveen." The words came back slowly, like water into a well. I passed, Rehana. Your Nani passed.

qa.q: How many professors were in the room at Parveen's viva?
qa.a: Three professors, with one creaking ceiling fan.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel when the mind went white?
qa.a: Parveen felt frozen with fear: hands stuck to the knees, a dry throat and a silence that felt endless.

qa.q: What turning point let Parveen answer again?
qa.a: Parveen breathed out longer than in, twice, and admitted aloud to going blank, which let the freeze thaw.

qa.q: How might the oldest professor have seen Parveen's silence?
qa.a: The professor seemed to see a nervous student rather than an unprepared one, and gave Parveen time to start again.

grounding: A young adult's mind goes blank in a viva, and slowing the breath and naming the moment aloud help it pass.

passage: Manoj had his bag on his shoulder and a train in forty minutes. "Thomas, the electricity bill. Three weeks now. Are you paying or not?" Out in the hostel corridor someone's speaker was booming, and every word Thomas had rehearsed disappeared. His jaw locked. His arms went stiff at his sides. He had lost his part-time shift and had only half the money, but his mouth wouldn't open. Manoj sighed loudly. Thomas pressed his feet into the floor and let one slow breath out, then another. "Sorry, I've frozen up," he said. "I've got half now. Can I pay the rest on Friday?" Manoj's shoulders dropped. "Why didn't you just say that?" "I couldn't, for a second." Manoj nodded and ran for his train.

qa.q: How long did Manoj have before his train?
qa.a: Manoj had a train in forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when his jaw locked?
qa.a: Thomas was overwhelmed and afraid; the rehearsed words vanished and his body went stiff.

qa.q: What helped Thomas get unstuck?
qa.a: Thomas pressed his feet into the floor, let out slow breaths and named the freeze aloud, then offered a clear plan for the money.

qa.q: How might Manoj have read Thomas's silence before Thomas spoke?
qa.a: Manoj may have taken it as dodging the bill, which is why he sighed loudly, until Thomas explained.

grounding: A young adult goes blank and stiff in a tense argument, and slowing the breath and naming the moment let him speak again.

passage: Okay, so you want the viva story. I'm Lavanya, and I'd been preparing for weeks. I walk in, three examiners, and the first question is easy, about my own project. And my mind goes white. Not nervous, Vandana. Blank. My hands were stuck to the table, my throat locked, and I could hear the clock. Ten seconds felt like ten minutes. Then I remembered something my hostel senior once told me: breathe out longer than you breathe in. So I did, twice. And I just said it: 'Sorry, I've gone blank. Give me a moment.' One examiner nodded and said, 'Take your time.' Saying it out loud somehow loosened everything. The first sentence came, then the next. I passed. Honestly, the naming-it part is what I tell everyone now.

qa.q: How many examiners were in the viva room?
qa.a: Three examiners.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when the blankness hit?
qa.a: Lavanya felt frozen and panicked, with hands stuck, throat locked and every second stretching.

qa.q: Which two things helped Lavanya recover?
qa.a: Breathing out longer than breathing in, and saying out loud that Lavanya had gone blank and needed a moment.

qa.q: What would change if the examiner had said, 'Come on, it's your own project'?
qa.a: Lavanya might have tightened up even more, and the freeze could have lasted longer.

grounding: Shows a young adult freezing in a viva, mind blank and body stiff, and how slowing the breath and naming the moment helps it pass.

passage:
Monday: In the bank interview, the panel asked Tanuja to talk about herself. Her mind went blank. She sat rigid, mouth dry, and finally said, 'I'm... sorry.' She left without finishing her answer and cried at the bus stop.
Thursday: Her friend Akash came over to practise. Each time she froze, he said, 'Stop. Breathe out slowly. Now say what's happening.' She felt silly saying, 'My mind's gone blank,' but after the fourth time, words came back faster.
The next Tuesday: At a second interview, the same blankness hit on a question about teamwork. Tanuja let out a long breath and said, 'Give me a second, I want to answer this properly.' The panel waited. Her shoulders loosened, and she told them about organising her college fest.

qa.q: What question did the panel ask Tanuja on Monday?
qa.a: To talk about herself.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling at the bus stop on Monday?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and upset after freezing, and cried.

qa.q: What did the practice with Akash teach Tanuja to do?
qa.a: To breathe out slowly and name what was happening, so the freeze eased instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Akash have seen his part in her progress?
qa.a: He probably felt glad and proud to see Tanuja's words come back faster each time she practised.

grounding: Shows a young adult freezing under interview pressure and learning over several days to thaw it by slowing the breath and naming the moment.

passage: Nikita, beta, you think I was always this talkative? Let your Chinmay Mama tell you something. When I was twenty-one, I told my father I wanted to leave engineering. He shouted, 'After all we've spent?' and I stood in the doorway, mouth dry, not a single word in my head. I had rehearsed for days, and it all vanished. My legs felt like wood. My father took my silence as agreement and walked away. For a month I said nothing more. Then one evening I tried again, and when the blankness came, I said, 'Baba, my mind has gone empty. Give me a few minutes.' I went to the balcony and breathed out slowly, again and again. When I came back, I could speak. He didn't agree that night. But he listened.

qa.q: How old was Chinmay when he told his father he wanted to leave engineering?
qa.a: Twenty-one.

qa.q: What was young Chinmay feeling as he stood in the doorway?
qa.a: He felt frozen and overwhelmed; the shouting made his rehearsed words vanish and his legs feel like wood.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chinmay's story?
qa.a: The evening he named the blankness aloud, asked for a few minutes and breathed slowly on the balcony before speaking again.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's father have understood the first silence?
qa.a: He took it as agreement, not realising his son had frozen under the shouting.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a young adult freezing in a heated argument and learning to thaw it by naming the moment and slowing the breath.

passage: Pooja's final-year viva was moved up by two hours, and she reached the department still panting from the auto, her notes left on the kitchen table. The external examiner asked a simple question about her own project, and her mind went white. Her hands turned cold, her throat locked, and the silence stretched. Through the glass door she caught Yamini's eye; Yamini pressed a hand to her own chest and breathed out slowly, the way they'd practised. Pooja did the same. 'I'm sorry,' she said. 'I've gone blank for a moment. Let me take a breath.' The examiner nodded. On the second slow breath the answer came back, and she explained her sampling method clearly.

qa.q: Where had Pooja left her notes?
qa.a: On the kitchen table.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when her mind went white?
qa.a: She felt panicked and frozen, with cold hands and a locked throat.

qa.q: What helped Pooja thaw?
qa.a: Slowing her breath as Yamini showed, and naming the moment aloud so she could pause.

qa.q: How might the examiner have seen Pooja's pause?
qa.a: The examiner likely saw ordinary nerves and respected the calm honesty of asking for a breath.

grounding: A young adult freezes in a viva, and slowing the breath and naming the moment thaws the stress reaction.
